topic: reviving an inherited pocket watch: mainspring, cap jewels, trace on the timing machine and poise

provenance.author: CC (batch EN-4)
provenance.notes: napisane niezaleznie, nie jest tlumaczeniem; urzadzenie obliczeniowe: timing machine (timegrapher), referent nieosadzony 'gate controller' celowo z innej dziedziny

base: I inherited a pocket watch from my grandfather and I would like it running properly again.
A spare movement of the same calibre sits in a tin on my bench.
A timing machine stands beside it and prints the rate on a narrow paper strip.
The watch runs for an hour or two and then stops without any obvious reason.
Should I start with the mainspring, or look first at the jewels and pivots?
Start with the mainspring, because a tired spring explains a stop far more often.
A spring that has set will drive the train for an hour and then falter.
Open the barrel and see whether the coils lie loosely against the barrel wall.
A healthy spring fills barely half the barrel when you lay it out flat.
The old spring almost filled the barrel and had clearly lost most of its set.
I fitted a new one and the watch has now run for a full day.
The timing machine prints a rate of about ninety seconds fast over each day.
The trace itself looks thick and ragged instead of forming one clean narrow line.
Is that thickness a jewel problem, or simply the regulator sitting too far over?
A ragged trace points at the jewels or the pivots, not at the regulator.
The regulator only shifts the whole trace up or down without changing its width.
Look at the balance jewels first, since a cracked cap jewel widens the trace.
Dried oil in the jewel holes gives much the same picture on the strip.
One cap jewel was indeed cracked across the middle and the oil had dried hard.
I took a sound cap jewel from the spare movement and cleaned both settings properly.
The trace is narrow now, though the rate still shows forty seconds fast daily.
Do I move the regulator, or is forty seconds a sign of something else?
Now the regulator is the right tool, because the trace has become clean again.
Move it a hair towards the slow mark and let the watch settle overnight.
Forty seconds is a small error and the regulator has plenty of range left.
Check the rate in several positions before you decide the job is finished.
The rate is now within five seconds a day when the watch lies flat.
Hanging in the pendant position, however, it loses nearly thirty seconds each day.
That difference seems large for a watch that has just been cleaned and oiled.
Is the balance out of poise, or should I suspect the pivots again?
A large vertical error usually means poise, though worn pivots can imitate it.
Check the pivots under magnification first, because that costs you nothing but time.
If they are round and polished, then the balance itself is out of poise.
Poising is delicate work and I would leave it until everything else is right.
The pivots look round under the loupe and both end stones are smooth.
So the balance must be heavy on one side, as you had guessed earlier.
I am reluctant to file the screws, since I have never poised a balance.
Would you leave thirty seconds alone, or is that too much to accept?
I would leave it, because a pocket watch spends most of its life vertical.
Regulate to the pendant position instead and let the flat rate run a little fast.
The watch will then keep good time in the pocket, where it actually lives.
Poising can wait until the next service, when the movement is apart anyway.
